title: A right in their wealth
hook: in their wealth was a right for the one who asks and the one deprived (51:19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, adh-dhariyat, and your line was by the scattering winds. What did you see the wind carry? Day five hundred ninety-four.

Two people stand outside a grocery store. One holds a cardboard sign and asks everyone who passes. The other, a few blocks away, has a job, an apartment, and an empty fridge she would never mention to anyone, not even her sister. The first is easy to see. The second you'd have to notice. The surah we opened yesterday names both of them, side by side, and it says something about money that changes what giving even is.

Verses fifteen to nineteen of Adh-Dhariyat describe the people of the gardens. They used to sleep little of the night. Before dawn, they asked forgiveness. And then verse nineteen, in Pickthall's translation: "And in their wealth the beggar and the outcast had due share." The Arabic puts it more bluntly. Wa fi amwalihim haqqun: and in their wealth, a right. Haqq means truth, and it also means what is owed, what someone is entitled to. So the poor don't receive a favor from these people. They receive what was already theirs, held for a while in someone else's account. Then the two who are owed. As-sa'il: the one who asks. And al-mahrum: the deprived. Ibn Kathir and other commentators explain the mahrum as the one in need who doesn't ask, whose dignity keeps them silent, who you'd have to notice to help. The verse puts the silent one right next to the asking one. A similar verse in Surah Al-Ma'arij says a known right, haqqun ma'lum, which some commentators connect to zakat, the fixed annual alms. Others read the verse here as reaching beyond it, to a generosity given on top of what was required. Notice the order of the verses: night prayer, then forgiveness before dawn, then wealth. In this passage, worship doesn't stay in the prayer room. For these people, it ended in their accounts. And the phrase offers a reframe. In the verse's terms, giving isn't a kindness done. It's a debt paid.
screen: `THE NIGHT PRAYER, THEN THE WEALTH.` · `HAQQ: TRUTH, AND WHAT IS OWED.` · `THE ONE WHO ASKS, AND THE ONE WHO WON'T.` · `NOT KINDNESS: A DEBT PAID.`

segments.voice: The practice: give to someone who didn't ask. Sit, and breathe. Think through the people around you, slowly: family, coworkers, neighbors, the friend who's gone quiet. Who might be struggling and not saying it? Look for small signs: skipped lunches, a canceled plan, a too-quick change of subject. Choose one person. Think of a way to give that protects their dignity: a meal you happened to make too much of, a gift card tucked in a card, help offered without fuss. If you pray, you can ask to notice. The bell holds the time.
Haqq: in 51:19, the share owed to the one who asks and to the deprived one who doesn't. Today's word.
Your line: a right, not a favor. Today, give something quietly to someone who didn't ask, and don't mention it afterward. Day five hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Muslims pay zakat, a fixed share of savings, once a year to set categories of people in need, and give voluntary sadaqah beyond it, often quietly, to protect the dignity of those who don't ask.

original.note: Arabic: truth; a right, what is owed.

trapdoor: what you thought: charity is generosity.
what it means: in 51:19, the poor have a right in your wealth; giving pays what's owed.
what a scholar hears: haqq means both truth and due; al-mahrum is explained as the needy one who doesn't ask; 70:24's 'known right' is linked to zakat.

sources.ref: Qur'an 51:15–18 (the people of the gardens: little sleep, forgiveness before dawn)

notes: Pickthall wording of 51:19 quoted from memory ('the beggar and the outcast had due share'); please confirm.
Commentators give several meanings of al-mahrum (one who doesn't ask, one with no share in spoils, one whose crop failed); the script uses the most common. Check.
Whether 51:19 refers to zakat or to voluntary giving beyond it: scholars differ (51 is Meccan, before zakat was fixed). Confirm the phrasing.
